screens.title: Advanced Concurrency: Locks and Atomic Variables
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we take a practical tour of Java’s advanced concurrency tools. You already know that the synchronized keyword gives you mutual exclusion tied to an object's monitor, but that simplicity sometimes limits flexibility. We’ll learn how explicit Lock objects, especially ReentrantLock, let you acquire and release locks across methods, attempt timed lock acquisition, and configure fairness. You’ll also see Condition objects, which unlock cleaner inter-thread signaling patterns than wait and notify. Finally, we’ll examine atomic variables like AtomicInteger that perform single-variable updates using hardware-supported compare-and-swap, enabling optimistic, lock-free updates for many high-throughput cases. Throughout the chapter we’ll use concrete code examples—a shared counter with ReentrantLock, a bounded buffer implementing producer-consumer with Conditions, and an AtomicInteger counter—to show both correct usage and common pitfalls. By the end you will know when synchronized suffices, when to prefer ReentrantLock and Conditions, and when atomic classes are the lighter, faster option. Think about a simple counter in your code: would you add a lock, or use an atomic variable? That question will guide many design choices you practice here.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Locks and atomics give you flexible, efficient tools for correct concurrency. Use them to avoid deadlocks, reduce contention, and implement precise inter-thread coordination.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Overview
Advanced Concurrency: Locks and Atomic Variables
Explicit locks give control. Atomic variables give speed. Both are tools you will choose depending on safety and throughput.
In this lesson

Explore ReentrantLock features, Condition-based signaling, and atomic variables with code walkthroughs and a hands-on refactor activity.

Why it matters

Correct concurrency reduces bugs and improves performance; these APIs help you choose the right trade-off between safety and throughput.

Explore Key Topics
Locks
ReentrantLock and tryLock for finer control
Conditions
await, signal, and multiple conditions for producer-consumer
Atomics
AtomicInteger and CAS for lock-free counters
Concept map
Locks → Conditions → Atomics
Mutual Exclusion
Lock-free Updates
Signaling
Fairness & Try-Lock
Quick example
Use ReentrantLock when you need interruptible waits, tryLock timeouts, or multiple Condition objects. Use AtomicInteger for a high-rate counter when only a single variable must be updated atomically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will be able to make practical decisions about synchronization in Java. First, you will explain the limitations of the synchronized keyword and why you might need explicit Lock objects. You will implement thread-safe code using ReentrantLock, including correct try-finally unlock patterns to avoid deadlocks. You will use Condition objects to express fine-grained waiting and signaling between threads, which is especially helpful in producer-consumer scenarios. You will also explain atomicity and the role of java. util. concurrent. atomic classes, and apply AtomicInteger to implement a high-performance counter without full locking. Each objective includes a hands-on component so you learn both the A P I and the common traps developers face with interrupted waits and missed signals. These skills matter because choosing the right synchronization primitive affects correctness and performance in real systems. Practice will focus on code patterns that scale well and avoid subtle concurrency bugs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills and checks
screens.narratorSegment: These additional objectives focus on making concurrency resilient and observable. You will practice acquiring and releasing ReentrantLock across different control flows, including releasing in finally blocks and responding to InterruptedException to keep threads cooperative. You will create and use multiple Condition objects for separate waiting conditions; that means writing code where producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty" and signaling only the relevant side. You will measure correctness by observing that consumers wait when buffers are empty and resume only when producers signal. Finally, you will test atomic counters under moderate contention and confirm that AtomicInteger incrementAndGet yields consistent results without synchronized blocks. Each objective includes checks such as ensuring no thread is left permanently blocked after exceptions and verifying final counter values match expected totals. Those checks make your concurrent code trustworthy in production.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Learning Checks
Practice checks
  • Ensure unlock() is always in finally even when InterruptedException occurs.
  • Use tryLock(timeout) when you must avoid indefinite blocking and handle failure paths cleanly.
  • When using Conditions, verify that await() actually releases the lock and that signalAll wakes the appropriate waiting threads.
  • Test AtomicInteger counters across multiple threads to confirm final totals match expected sums.
Misconception checks
  • Don’t assume configuring ReentrantLock as fair always improves throughput; it reduces starvation at a potential throughput cost.
  • AtomicInteger does not protect complex object graphs—only single variables.
  • Condition.signalAll() is not a substitute for correct condition predicates inside while loops.
Try this
Refactor a simple bank account to use a ReentrantLock and one Condition. Observe that withdrawals wait and only proceed after deposits signal the condition.

screens.title: Limitations of synchronized
screens.narratorSegment: The synchronized keyword is simple: it ties a lock to an object's monitor and scopes the lock to the enclosing block or method. That block-structured nature is a feature for clarity but a limitation when you need flexibility across call boundaries. A synchronized block must be released in the same lexical scope where it was acquired. This makes patterns like acquiring a lock in one method and releasing it later in another method impossible with synchronized. It also means you have limited control over how a thread acquires a lock: you cannot attempt a timed try, you cannot be interrupted while waiting for the monitor, and you cannot attach multiple distinct condition queues to the same lock. A typical misconception is that synchronized and explicit locks are interchangeable; in fact, explicit locks unlock patterns like tryLock with timeout and lockInterruptibly that let your thread react to interrupts or back out when contention is high. For example, in a long-running operation you might prefer interruptible waits to allow cooperative cancellation. Keep in mind synchronized still buys simplicity and low ceremony, so it remains a good default for many simple cases. The practical rule: use synchronized for straightforward, short critical sections and reach for explicit locks when you need finer control, timed acquisition, or multiple condition queues.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Limitations of synchronized
Definition

Synchronized is an intrinsic, block-structured lock bound to an object's monitor. It requires acquisition and release within the same block or method.

Common misconception
Many assume synchronized can be interrupted or tried with a timeout; it cannot.
When it still fits
  • Short, simple critical sections.
  • Methods where lock scope is local and obvious.
  • No need for timed waits or multiple conditions.
Practical contrast
What you can’t do with synchronized
  • Acquire in one method and release in another.
  • Use tryLock(time) to back off on contention.
  • Attach multiple condition queues to the same lock.
When to migrate to ReentrantLock
If you need interruptible acquisition, timed locks, explicit fairness, or multiple Conditions, prefer ReentrantLock.
Key Takeaway

Synchronized works well for simple cases. Use explicit locks when you need control beyond block-scoped mutual exclusion.

screens.title: ReentrantLock: features and behaviors
screens.narratorSegment: ReentrantLock implements the Lock interface and offers the same mutual exclusion guarantee as synchronized but with added, practical features. First, locks are non-block-structured: you can acquire a lock in one method and release it in another, which is helpful for stateful protocols. Second, acquisition can be interruptible; a thread blocked waiting for a lock can respond to an interrupt when using lockInterruptibly. Third, tryLock with optional timeout enables a thread to attempt acquisition and otherwise do alternative work, preventing indefinite blocking and enabling graceful degradation. Fourth, ReentrantLock can be constructed with a fairness policy. A fair lock hands the lock to the longest-waiting thread, reducing starvation at a potential throughput cost. Finally, a ReentrantLock can create multiple Condition objects so different wait sets can be signaled independently. These features let you design more responsive and maintainable concurrency protocols. A common mistake is forgetting that fairness may slow throughput or failing to use try-finally to ensure unlock always runs; both are emphasized in the code examples you will study. ReentrantLock: features and behaviors means use reentrantlock for timed acquisition, interruptible waits, fairness options, and multiple condition objects.. In practical terms, what reentrantlock gives you beyond synchronized. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › ReentrantLock Features
1. Non-block-structured
Lock can be acquired and released in different call frames, enabling protocol-style concurrency patterns.
2. Interruptible acquisition
lockInterruptibly allows a waiting thread to be interrupted, improving responsiveness and avoiding some deadlocks.
3. tryLock and fairness
tryLock lets you attempt a lock with timeout. Fair locks reduce starvation but may lower throughput.
4. Multiple Condition objects
Attach multiple Conditions per lock to separate wait sets for clear signaling.
Practical example pattern
When you need producers and consumers to wait on distinct conditions, create two Condition objects from the same ReentrantLock, and signal only the side that should proceed. Combine tryLock or lockInterruptibly with a timeout to avoid threads stuck indefinitely if an external shutdown is requested.
Pro tip
Always wrap lock acquisition and critical work in try-finally to guarantee unlock(). Forgetting unlock is a primary source of deadlocks.

screens.title: ReentrantLock example: SharedResourceWithLock
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete ReentrantLock example that shows the correct pattern for acquiring and releasing a lock. In the provided SharedResourceWithLock code, a final ReentrantLock is used to guard a simple integer counter. Each increment begins with lock. lock(); the critical section updates the counter and simulates work. Crucially, the unlock call sits in a finally block so that even if an InterruptedException is thrown, the lock is always released. This prevents permanent blocking by other threads. The example also shows protecting reads with the same lock so that getCounter() returns a consistent value. A common beginner mistake is calling unlock without ensuring the current thread actually holds the lock; always structure code so unlock runs only after a successful lock acquisition. Another pitfall is swallowing interrupts; when an InterruptedException occurs, set the thread's interrupt status so higher-level cancellation logic can run. Finally, observe that this pattern is best for protecting small critical sections—if you hold the lock while doing long input and output, you will serialize too much work and lose concurrency benefits. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › SharedResourceWithLock
Code
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class SharedResourceWithLock {
  private int counter = 0;
  private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(); // Create a ReentrantLock

  public void increment() {
    lock.lock(); // Acquire the lock
    try {
      // Critical section
      counter++;
      System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " incremented to: " + counter);
      Thread.sleep(50); // Simulate work
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
      Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    } finally {
      lock.unlock(); // Always release the lock in a finally block
    }
  }

  public int getCounter() {
    lock.lock(); // Acquire lock for read access too
    try {
      return counter;
    } finally {
      lock.unlock();
    }
  }
}
Explanation
  • lock.lock() acquires the lock; unlock() in finally ensures release even on exceptions.
  • Protect both read and write methods to avoid observing inconsistent state.
  • Simulated work inside the critical section shows why sections should remain small.
Common mistake
Forgetting unlock() or calling unlock() from a thread that doesn't hold the lock leads to IllegalMonitorStateException or deadlock.
Key Takeaway

Use try-finally for safety and keep critical sections short to preserve concurrency.

screens.title: Unlocking, exceptions, and deadlocks
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent source of concurrency bugs is failing to release a lock when exceptions occur. Always release locks in a finally block so that other threads are not blocked forever. Deadlocks occur when two or more threads each hold locks that the others need; for example, Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y while Thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. While ReentrantLock can't prevent deadlocks by itself, using tryLock with timeouts or lockInterruptibly can reduce the chance that threads remain blocked indefinitely by enabling a thread to back off or respond to interrupts. Another practical defense is lock ordering: always acquire multiple locks in a consistent global order. A misconception is thinking that tryLock guarantees liveness; it only gives you the opportunity to handle the failed acquisition. Design choices such as reducing lock scope, using finer-grained locks, or switching to lock-free atomics for single-variable updates are often the most effective ways to avoid deadlock and improve throughput. Unlocking, exceptions, and deadlocks means release locks in finally, prefer consistent lock ordering, and use trylock or interrupts to let threads back out when necessary.. In practical terms, why releasing locks in finally matters and how deadlocks arise. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Deadlocks & Unlock
How deadlocks form
  • Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y.
  • Thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X.
  • Neither can proceed, causing a system stall.
Defenses
  • Use tryLock with timeout to back off when acquisition fails.
  • Use lockInterruptibly to allow cancellation.
  • Keep lock scopes small and enforce lock ordering.
Common mistake
Calling unlock outside of finally or skipping interrupt handling can leave a lock held forever, blocking progress.
Pro tip
If you must hold multiple locks, define a global acquisition order and stick to it in all code paths.
Check your understanding
Can your code be interrupted while waiting for a lock? If not, consider lockInterruptibly or a tryLock with timeout.

screens.title: Condition objects and await/signal
screens.narratorSegment: Condition objects provide an alternative to Object. wait() and notify() by being explicitly tied to a Lock instance. A Condition lets threads wait for a particular predicate while releasing the associated lock, and later be signaled when that predicate might hold. The advantages are twofold: first, you can create multiple Condition objects per lock to represent distinct wait sets, for instance one for 'notEmpty' and another for 'notFull' in a bounded buffer. Second, using Conditions makes the waiting and signaling semantics clearer and reduces accidental notification of unrelated waiters. Remember that Condition. await() releases the lock and suspends the thread until signaled, at which point it reacquires the lock before returning. A common mistake is calling signal or signalAll without holding the lock; do so while still holding the lock to avoid lost wakeups. Also, always wait inside a loop that checks the predicate since spurious wakeups can occur. With these patterns you build robust producer-consumer code that avoids missed signals and reduces contention by signaling only the responsible party. Condition objects and await/signal means use condition objects tied to a lock to create precise wait sets and avoid the pitfalls of coarse notifyall usage.. In practical terms, how conditions improve wait/notify semantics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Condition Objects
How it works
A Condition is created from a Lock. When a thread calls await(), it atomically releases the associated lock and suspends. When signaled, the thread wakes and reacquires the lock before returning. Multiple Conditions let you separate different wait reasons for the same lock.
Rule
Always wait inside a while loop that checks the condition to handle spurious wakeups and re-check predicates.
Do not forget
Call signal() or signalAll() while holding the same lock to avoid lost notifications.
Concrete scenario
In a bounded buffer, use notFull for producers and notEmpty for consumers so that a producer only wakes consumers and vice versa, leading to cleaner coordination than using notifyAll.
Key Takeaway

Conditions give precise control over which threads are signaled and maintain the lock-release semantics needed for safe waiting.

screens.title: BoundedBuffer: Producer-Consumer with Conditions
screens.narratorSegment: The BoundedBuffer example demonstrates using a ReentrantLock plus two Condition objects to coordinate producers and consumers. The buffer holds a queue with a fixed capacity. In put(), the producer acquires the lock and checks the predicate buffer. size() == capacity in a while loop; if full, it calls notFull. await(), which releases the lock and suspends the thread. When it can add the item, it signals notEmpty. signalAll() so waiting consumers can wake. In take(), the consumer similarly waits on notEmpty until there is data, then removes an item and signals notFull. signalAll() to wake producers. The use of while loops ensures robustness to spurious wakeups. Notice that await() releases the lock while waiting and reacquires it before returning, preserving mutual exclusion when accessing the shared queue. This pattern avoids the broad notifyAll approach and instead targets the appropriate wait set. In practice, signalAll is often used to simplify correctness; focused signal() can be used when you can guarantee a single waiter should proceed. Running the example with producer and consumer tasks reveals orderly waiting and resumption and demonstrates how Conditions make reasoning clear.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › BoundedBuffer Example
Code
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.Queue;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

class BoundedBuffer {
  private final Queue buffer = new LinkedList<>();
  private final int capacity;
  private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
  private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); // consumers
  private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();  // producers

  public BoundedBuffer(int capacity) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
  }

  public void put(int item) throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
      while (buffer.size() == capacity) {
        System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": Buffer full, waiting to put " + item);
        notFull.await(); // Wait until buffer is not full
      }
      buffer.add(item);
      System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": Put " + item + ", size: " + buffer.size());
      notEmpty.signalAll(); // Signal consumers that buffer is not empty
    } finally {
      lock.unlock();
    }
  }

  public int take() throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
      while (buffer.isEmpty()) {
        System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": Buffer empty, waiting to take.");
        notEmpty.await(); // Wait until buffer is not empty
      }
      int item = buffer.remove();
      System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + ": Took " + item + ", size: " + buffer.size());
      notFull.signalAll(); // Signal producers that buffer is not full
      return item;
    } finally {
      lock.unlock();
    }
  }
}
Explanation
Producers await notFull; consumers await notEmpty. Each await releases the lock while suspended. Use while loops so the predicate is rechecked after wake-up.
Behavioral note
signalAll is safe and simple. If you can guarantee a single waiter, signal() reduces wakeups but requires careful reasoning.
Key Takeaway

Conditions let you express separate waiting reasons and implement robust producer-consumer queues with clear signaling.

screens.title: Condition await and signal lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the lifecycle of await and signal clarifies why Conditions must be used with care. Step one: a thread acquires the lock and checks the condition predicate; if the predicate is false, it calls await(). At await(), the condition subsystem atomically releases the lock and suspends the thread. Step two: another thread acquires the lock, changes shared state in a way that may make the predicate true, and calls signal() or signalAll() while still holding the lock. Step three: signaling moves waiting threads to a runnable state, but they must reacquire the lock before returning from await(). That means a signaled thread won't proceed until it reacquires the lock; this preserves mutual exclusion. Use a while loop around await() to re-evaluate the predicate after reacquiring the lock because spurious wakeups or intervening actions may have invalidated the condition again. Misunderstanding the reacquire step leads developers to assume a signaled thread immediately runs the critical section; in fact it still competes to reacquire the lock. This sequence explains why Condition-based protocols maintain safety and why signal timing and lock hold semantics matter.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Await & Signal Flow
Step-by-step
  1. Check predicate: If false, call await() inside a while loop.
  2. Await: Releases the lock and suspends the thread atomically.
  3. Modify state: Another thread changes shared state and calls signal()/signalAll() while holding the lock.
  4. Reacquire: Signaled threads try to reacquire the lock and re-check the predicate when they resume.
Why while-loops?
Spurious wakeups or a different thread consuming the condition could leave the predicate false even after a wake; recheck to remain safe.
Key Takeaway

Treat signal as a hint that the predicate may be true; always re-evaluate under the lock.

screens.title: Atomicity and atomic variables
screens.narratorSegment: Atomicity means an operation appears to happen instantaneously and completely to all threads. Atomic classes in java. util. concurrent. atomic provide operations on single variables that are atomic without using locks. For example, AtomicInteger. incrementAndGet() performs an atomic increment so no two threads can observe or produce lost updates for that single variable. These classes rely on a low-level Compare-And-Swap primitive provided by hardware. A CAS operation tests whether a memory location contains an expected value and, if so, updates it to a new value in one atomic step; it returns whether the swap succeeded. This enables optimistic locking: a thread reads a value, computes a new value, then attempts a CAS. If the CAS fails because another thread modified the value, the thread retries. Optimistic locking shines when contention is low and the cost of retries is less than the cost of blocking. However, atomic variables only protect single variables and cannot replace full synchronization when multiple related pieces of state must be updated together. Atomicity and atomic variables means atomicinteger and friends provide lock-free, single-variable atomic operations using cas, ideal for counters and simple flags under moderate contention.. In practical terms, what atomic operations mean and when to use them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Atomicity & CAS
Definition

An atomic operation completes as a single, indivisible action from the perspective of other threads. Atomic classes use CAS to implement these operations without locks.

Optimistic vs Pessimistic
  • Optimistic: Try an update and retry on conflict (CAS).
  • Pessimistic: Acquire a lock before modifying shared state.
When to use atomics
  • Single-variable counters or flags.
  • High-throughput increments where blocking costs are too high.
  • When combined updates across multiple variables are not required.
Key Takeaway

Use atomics for single-variable lock-free updates; use locks when you must update multiple related fields consistently.

AtomicInteger exposes incrementAndGet() to perform an atomic increment and return the updated value. Under moderate contention this avoids the cost of locking entirely and uses the hardware compare-and-swap loop internally. In the example, multiple threads repeatedly call increment, and at the end the final counter value should equal the sum of all increments. A common misconception is thinking AtomicInteger replaces locks for all concurrency needs; it only guarantees atomicity for that single integer. If you need to update an account balance and a transaction log atomically together, atomics alone are insufficient. Another nuance is that a CAS loop can spin and retry under heavy contention, which degrades performance; in those scenarios a blocking lock may perform better. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › AtomicCounter
Code
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

public class AtomicCounter {
  private AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger(0); // Use AtomicInteger

  public void increment() {
    counter.incrementAndGet(); // Atomic increment
    System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " incremented to: " + counter.get());
  }

  public int getCounter() {
    return counter.get();
  }
}
Explanation
incrementAndGet performs a single atomic operation. No explicit lock is used, so this is efficient under moderate contention.
Limitations
AtomicInteger cannot protect updates spanning multiple variables; use locks for multi-field invariants.
Key Takeaway

Atomic variables provide a compact, fast alternative to locks for single-variable updates but do not replace full synchronization for complex state.

screens.title: Pessimistic vs Optimistic locking
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between pessimistic and optimistic locking comes down to expected contention and the complexity of the update. Pessimistic locking, like synchronized or ReentrantLock, assumes contention will occur and prevents concurrent access by blocking other threads. This is the safe choice when you must update multiple related variables together or when invariants require exclusive access. Optimistic locking, implemented via CAS-based atomic variables, assumes contention is rare. Threads attempt updates without blocking and retry only if conflicts occur. Optimistic locking is very efficient when updates are frequent but contention is low, such as incrementing a global metric. However, if contention is high and CAS retries proliferate, performance can drop and spinning wastes C P U. Another tradeoff is complexity: optimistic patterns can complicate multi-step updates unless you redesign state into single-update atoms or use versioning. A practical rule of thumb: start with atomics for single-variable counters, use locks for compound invariants, and measure under realistic contention to guide tuning. Pessimistic vs Optimistic locking means use optimistic atomics for single-variable, low-contention updates; use locks for compound operations and high-contention correctness.. Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Pessimistic vs Optimistic
Pessimistic (Locks)
  • Blocks other threads to maintain invariants.
  • Good for compound updates across multiple fields.
  • Can cause blocking and context switches under contention.
Optimistic (Atomics)
  • Uses CAS to attempt updates without blocking.
  • Efficient for single-variable updates when contention is low.
  • Retries can be costly under heavy contention.
Decision checklist
Single variable?
Low contention?
Compound invariants?
If the first two are true, prefer atomics. If compound invariants exist, prefer locks.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.5 › Refactor Activity
Starter template
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Condition;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock;
import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock;

public class ConcurrentBankAccount {
  private double balance;
  private final Lock accountLock = new ReentrantLock();
  private final Condition sufficientFunds = accountLock.newCondition();

  public ConcurrentBankAccount(double initialBalance) {
    this.balance = initialBalance;
  }

  public void deposit(double amount) throws InterruptedException {
    accountLock.lock();
    try {
      // Implement deposit logic with signalAll()
      System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " deposited " + amount + ", new balance: " + balance);
      Thread.sleep(50);
    } finally {
      accountLock.unlock();
    }
  }

  public void withdraw(double amount) throws InterruptedException {
    accountLock.lock();
    try {
      // Implement withdraw logic with await() and signalAll()
      System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " withdrew " + amount + ", new balance: " + balance);
      Thread.sleep(50);
    } finally {
      accountLock.unlock();
    }
  }

  public double getBalance() {
    accountLock.lock();
    try {
      return balance;
    } finally {
      accountLock.unlock();
    }
  }
}
Refactor steps
  1. Acquire lock before modifying balance.
  2. In withdraw, while(balance < amount) call sufficientFunds.await().
  3. In deposit, after adding amount, call sufficientFunds.signalAll().
Why this helps
Withdrawals wait efficiently and are only woken when funds could be sufficient, giving clearer, safer coordination than busy waits.
Key Takeaway

Use Conditions to signal the exact waiting party and always protect state changes with the associated lock.

Each of these tools has trade-offs: explicit locks buy flexibility at the cost of more careful management, Conditions allow clearer signaling than wait/notify but require correct use of while loops, and atomics are fast but cannot replace locks for compound updates. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we take a practical tour of Java’s advanced concurrency tools. You already know that the synchronized keyword gives you mutual exclusion tied to an object's monitor, but that simplicity sometimes limits flexibility. We’ll learn how explicit Lock objects, especially ReentrantLock, let you acquire and release locks across methods, attempt timed lock acquisition, and configure fairness. You’ll also see Condition objects, which unlock cleaner inter-thread signaling patterns than wait and notify. Finally, we’ll examine atomic variables like AtomicInteger that perform single-variable updates using hardware-supported compare-and-swap, enabling optimistic, lock-free updates for many high-throughput cases. Throughout the chapter we’ll use concrete code examples—a shared counter with ReentrantLock, a bounded buffer implementing producer-consumer with Conditions, and an AtomicInteger counter—to show both correct usage and common pitfalls. By the end you will know when synchronized suffices, when to prefer ReentrantLock and Conditions, and when atomic classes are the lighter, faster option. Think about a simple counter in your code: would you add a lock, or use an atomic variable? That question will guide many design choices you practice here.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to make practical decisions about synchronization in Java. First, you will explain the limitations of the synchronized keyword and why you might need explicit Lock objects. You will implement thread-safe code using ReentrantLock, including correct try-finally unlock patterns to avoid deadlocks. You will use Condition objects to express fine-grained waiting and signaling between threads, which is especially helpful in producer-consumer scenarios. You will also explain atomicity and the role of java. util. concurrent. atomic classes, and apply AtomicInteger to implement a high-performance counter without full locking. Each objective includes a hands-on component so you learn both the A P I and the common traps developers face with interrupted waits and missed signals. These skills matter because choosing the right synchronization primitive affects correctness and performance in real systems. Practice will focus on code patterns that scale well and avoid subtle concurrency bugs.

These additional objectives focus on making concurrency resilient and observable. You will practice acquiring and releasing ReentrantLock across different control flows, including releasing in finally blocks and responding to InterruptedException to keep threads cooperative. You will create and use multiple Condition objects for separate waiting conditions; that means writing code where producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty" and signaling only the relevant side. You will measure correctness by observing that consumers wait when buffers are empty and resume only when producers signal. Finally, you will test atomic counters under moderate contention and confirm that AtomicInteger incrementAndGet yields consistent results without synchronized blocks. Each objective includes checks such as ensuring no thread is left permanently blocked after exceptions and verifying final counter values match expected totals. Those checks make your concurrent code trustworthy in production.

The synchronized keyword is simple: it ties a lock to an object's monitor and scopes the lock to the enclosing block or method. That block-structured nature is a feature for clarity but a limitation when you need flexibility across call boundaries. A synchronized block must be released in the same lexical scope where it was acquired. This makes patterns like acquiring a lock in one method and releasing it later in another method impossible with synchronized. It also means you have limited control over how a thread acquires a lock: you cannot attempt a timed try, you cannot be interrupted while waiting for the monitor, and you cannot attach multiple distinct condition queues to the same lock. A typical misconception is that synchronized and explicit locks are interchangeable; in fact, explicit locks unlock patterns like tryLock with timeout and lockInterruptibly that let your thread react to interrupts or back out when contention is high. For example, in a long-running operation you might prefer interruptible waits to allow cooperative cancellation. Keep in mind synchronized still buys simplicity and low ceremony, so it remains a good default for many simple cases. The practical rule: use synchronized for straightforward, short critical sections and reach for explicit locks when you need finer control, timed acquisition, or multiple condition queues.

ReentrantLock implements the Lock interface and offers the same mutual exclusion guarantee as synchronized but with added, practical features. First, locks are non-block-structured: you can acquire a lock in one method and release it in another, which is helpful for stateful protocols. Second, acquisition can be interruptible; a thread blocked waiting for a lock can respond to an interrupt when using lockInterruptibly. Third, tryLock with optional timeout enables a thread to attempt acquisition and otherwise do alternative work, preventing indefinite blocking and enabling graceful degradation. Fourth, ReentrantLock can be constructed with a fairness policy. A fair lock hands the lock to the longest-waiting thread, reducing starvation at a potential throughput cost. Finally, a ReentrantLock can create multiple Condition objects so different wait sets can be signaled independently. These features let you design more responsive and maintainable concurrency protocols. A common mistake is forgetting that fairness may slow throughput or failing to use try-finally to ensure unlock always runs; both are emphasized in the code examples you will study. ReentrantLock: features and behaviors means use reentrantlock for timed acquisition, interruptible waits, fairness options, and multiple condition objects.. In practical terms, what reentrantlock gives you beyond synchronized. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. A frequent source of concurrency bugs is failing to release a lock when exceptions occur. Always release locks in a finally block so that other threads are not blocked forever. Deadlocks occur when two or more threads each hold locks that the others need; for example, Thread A holds lock X and waits for lock Y while Thread B holds lock Y and waits for lock X. A Condition lets threads wait for a particular predicate while releasing the associated lock, and later be signaled when that predicate might hold. Also, always wait inside a loop that checks the predicate since spurious wakeups can occur. Understanding the lifecycle of await and signal clarifies why Conditions must be used with care. Step one: a thread acquires the lock and checks the condition predicate; if the predicate is false, it calls await(). Atomicity means an operation appears to happen instantaneously and completely to all threads. Atomic classes in java. util. concurrent. atomic provide operations on single variables that are atomic without using locks. For example, AtomicInteger. incrementAndGet() performs an atomic increment so no two threads can observe or produce lost updates for that single variable. These classes rely on a low-level Compare-And-Swap primitive provided by hardware. A CAS operation tests whether a memory location contains an expected value and, if so, updates it to a new value in one atomic step; it returns whether the swap succeeded. This enables optimistic locking: a thread reads a value, computes a new value, then attempts a CAS. If the CAS fails because another thread modified the value, the thread retries. Optimistic locking shines when contention is low and the cost of retries is less than the cost of blocking. However, atomic variables only protect single variables and cannot replace full synchronization when multiple related pieces of state must be updated together. Choosing between pessimistic and optimistic locking comes down to expected contention and the complexity of the update. Pessimistic locking, like synchronized or ReentrantLock, assumes contention will occur and prevents concurrent access by blocking other threads. This is the safe choice when you must update multiple related variables together or when invariants require exclusive access. Optimistic locking, implemented via CAS-based atomic variables, assumes contention is rare. Threads attempt updates without blocking and retry only if conflicts occur. Optimistic locking is very efficient when updates are frequent but contention is low, such as incrementing a global metric. However, if contention is high and CAS retries proliferate, performance can drop and spinning wastes C P U. Another tradeoff is complexity: optimistic patterns can complicate multi-step updates unless you redesign state into single-update atoms or use versioning. A practical rule of thumb: start with atomics for single-variable counters, use locks for compound invariants, and measure under realistic contention to guide tuning. Here are the core ideas to carry forward. ReentrantLock: an explicit lock that supports non-block-structured acquisition, interruptible waits, tryLock with timeouts, and optional fairness—useful when you need fine control. Condition objects: obtained from a Lock, they let you create multiple, specific wait sets and use await and signal to coordinate producers and consumers reliably. Each of these tools has trade-offs: explicit locks buy flexibility at the cost of more careful management, Conditions allow clearer signaling than wait/notify but require correct use of while loops, and atomics are fast but cannot replace locks for compound updates. Third, for simple counters prefer AtomicInteger for high throughput, but use locks when you must maintain complex, multi-field invariants.
